I am a 45-year-old woman who has farmed these 10 mu in Quzhou for 20 years. I never went to school, but I have watched the seasons turn and learned from my neighbors and from my own mistakes. My household has seven people, and some of my family work off-farm, which brings in cash but means I cannot afford to waste labor. I have a well, so when the crops need water, I can irrigate.

For my winter wheat, I always plant the full 10.1 mu because it is our staple crop and the land would sit empty otherwise. I till the soil with a rotary tiller before sowing in October, and I use an improved variety like the ones my neighbors use—Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22. I sow about 30 jin of seed per mu. For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer as a base and then topdress with nitrogen in the spring. After all these years, I know that about 18 kg of nitrogen, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium per mu gives a good crop without throwing money away. Because I have the well, I irrigate four times: once to help the wheat overwinter, once when it greens up, once at jointing, and once during grain filling. I also spray four times for weeds, insects, and disease—if I skip it, the bugs will eat everything. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat if the weather is fair.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I immediately plant summer maize. Everyone here uses hybrid maize now—Denghai 605 or something like it—because the hybrids yield much more than the old kinds. I plant about one package of seed per mu. Time is short between wheat harvest and maize sowing, and with some of my family away working, I use no-tillage direct seeding. I put down compound fertilizer at sowing, about 11 kg of nitrogen, 3 kg of phosphorus, and 3 kg of potassium per mu. Maize in summer usually gets some rain, but I irrigate twice—at jointing and at filling—to make sure the ears fill out properly. I spray three times for pests and weeds. If things go normally, I should get about 550 kg per mu from the maize.
